items.content:
Data scaling and compute scaling are *multipliers* for the generalization power of an approach. Trillions of dollars in investment can make very inefficient, low-generalization approaches look adequate, but that doesn't make them the ultimate end-all-be-all of AI.

You should work on methods that *can* scale, because if you don't benefit from this multiplier you simply can't compete. But you should keep in mind scaling is only a multiplier: a cleverer approach will scale *better*.

items.content:
@gabriberton Several comments:
1. image/video SSL methods differ by whether they use reconstruction or not. Joint embedding architectures Amy or may not have a predictor (JEA vs JEPA). They also differ by their anti-collapse method and data corruption/augmentation methods.
2. DINO *is* a kind of JEPA (technically a JEA). The difference with other JEPA models is the anti-collapse criterion (based on contrative clustering+ stopgradient/EMA), and the data augmentation scheme (image transformations, which is task specific),
3. V-JEPA 2.1, like DINO, is from Meta-FAIR (corporate lab), involved significant engineering teams, large/proprietary datasets, considerable computing resources, lots of fine-tuning, and number-pushing on many benchmarks.
4. Many JEPA papers are applications and/or fine-tuned versions of DINO, V-JEPA or I-JEPA.
5. LeJEPA, LeWM, and most other papers with "JEPA" in the title are *research* papers focused on the methodology, often done by students in academic labs, involving no engineering support, very little computing resources, and small/public training sets. They are generally tested on toy problems, simulated environments, or small/public benchmarks.
6. You simply cannot compare 5 with 2/3/4. 5 gives you ideas and new methods, not models. 2/3 give you well-engineered models, with lots of empirically validated tricks. Only rarely will 2/3 give you a new, well-principled method with room to spare. 5 give you empirical results on new applications.
7. What is published in 5 are methods that will eventually become like 2 and 3, whenever someone with resources picks it up and scales it.

DO NOT CONFUSE UPSTREAM FOUNDATIONAL RESEARCH ON METHODS AND DOWNSTREAM SCALING -> ENGINEERING -> NUMBER PUSHING -> MODELS -> PRODUCTS.
The former makes the rest possible, but it takes time.

items.content:
Claude Code can design furniture part by part and then give you a bill of materials to order each part and put it together yourself 

And way cheaper than big interior brands sell you their furniture

Furnishing my house I discovered how absolutely insane prices are for the most basic cheap materials put together with a fancy brand tied to it

One shop had a sofa for $30,000 😂

I think with Opus 5.5 and other models easily operating 3d programs like Blender and FreeCAD (both free) it makes more sense to cut out the middle man and go straight to suppliers and design and build your own furniture

Which in a way makes customers more powerful (they can get exactly what they want and usually for cheaper without the markup)

Anyway @theannalux designed this table from scratch, she's not a furniture designer, not a coder, she just had an idea of a style and worked with Claude Code in the terminal (far superior to the app I will keep saying this)

If you design your own furniture and buy the raw materials directly, you can save 85% compared to premium brands like Poliform

That means the $30,000 sofa becomes $4,500! And the $8,000 dinner table becomes just $1,200!

You can see where the idea comes from that AI will make everything 5x to 20x cheaper, and it's already starting!

The field of artificial intelligence, data science, and analytics is crippling itself. Exaggerated promises of unrealistic technologies, simplifications of complex projects, and marketing hype are leading to an erosion of trust in one of our most critical approaches to making decisions: data driven.

This book aims to fix this by countering the AI hype with a dose of realism. Written by two experts in the field, the authors firmly believe in the power of mathematics, computing, and analytics, but if false expectations are set and practitioners and leaders don’t fully understand everything that really goes into data science projects, then a stunning 80% (or more) of analytics projects will continue to fail, costing enterprises and society hundreds of billions of dollars, and leading to non-experts abandoning one of the most important data-driven decision-making capabilities altogether.

For the first time, business leaders, practitioners, students, and interested laypeople will learn what really makes a data science project successful. By illustrating with many personal stories, the authors reveal the harsh realities of implementing AI and analytics.

items.content:
Autonomous software agents operating in graphical user interfaces face severe risks during execution. Unlike text generation, interacting with desktop software involves high operational latency, context-dependent or irreversible actions, and the threat of corrupting critical documents. Because real-time trial-and-error exploration is dangerous and impractical in production environments, agents require a mechanism to forecast the outcomes of their choices before executing them.

The article introduces and evaluates the Computer-Using World Model, an environment simulator designed specifically for desktop applications. The primary objective is to demonstrate that explicitly modeling software user-interface dynamics allows autonomous agents to safely simulate candidate actions during inference, thereby improving decision-making accuracy and robustness without retraining the underlying agent policies.

items.title: Computer-use agents often work through interfaces designed in advance by people, such as screenshots...
items.content:
Computer-use agents often work through interfaces designed in advance by people, such as screenshots, clicks, and keystrokes. These fixed interfaces can make routine tasks slow or unreliable, even when a more direct way to inspect or change application data is available. Improving them typically requires researchers to diagnose failures and build new tools by hand. The article asks whether agents can instead use their own task experience to develop reusable interfaces, without changing the task agent’s underlying model or execution framework.

The article introduces Agent S4, a system that evolves a repository of executable interfaces and guidance on when to use them. A fixed task agent attempts synthetic computer-use tasks, producing interaction histories but no ground-truth success labels. A separate meta-agent studies those histories and proposes interface or guidance changes. It can revise one repository or combine ideas from two. Held-out validation results determine which variants are selected for further development, but the meta-agent cannot see validation tasks, trajectories, or scores while making changes. The researchers tested the approach on OSWorld V2, a benchmark of 108 desktop workflows, and ScienceBoard, a 169-task benchmark involving specialized scientific applications. Each search involved 30 repository changes; construction used 30 synthetic tasks for OSWorld V2 and 48 for ScienceBoard, with 15 official tasks per benchmark reserved for validation.

items.title: As web information changes, language models quickly become outdated, while rebuilding them from scra...
items.content:
As web information changes, language models quickly become outdated, while rebuilding them from scratch is prohibitively expensive. The article evaluates whether continued pretraining on newer web data can update a model’s factual knowledge while preserving what it already knows and can do. It studies a realistic update setting: successive web crawls overlap with earlier material, rather than forming completely separate data streams.

The researchers continued pretraining six open models, ranging from 1 billion to 8 billion parameters across three model families, using English educational web data published after each model’s knowledge cutoff. They compared a curated 6-billion-token data slice with a broader 40-billion-token slice. They measured changes in answers to news-based questions from before and after each cutoff, performance on 13 general-purpose tasks, and the effects of different training settings. They also tested whether the gains remained after instruction tuning and preference optimization.

items.title: Curated language-model benchmarks often use clean, controlled examples that do not reflect the ambig...
items.content:
Curated language-model benchmarks often use clean, controlled examples that do not reflect the ambiguity and contextual clutter of real financial, biomedical, and legal work. As a result, strong benchmark scores may offer limited assurance about performance in deployment. The article addresses how to make existing test cases more demanding without changing what counts as the correct answer—a key safeguard against mistaking broken or misleading test cases for genuine robustness failures.

The article introduces HARDEN, a method that repeatedly generates and tests realistic variations of existing benchmark inputs while keeping their expected answers fixed. It searches for changes that make a selected language model less accurate and less certain, and filters candidates for preservation of answer-relevant evidence, domain realism, and technical validity. The authors tested it on 200 cases each from FinQA, PubMedQA, and ContractNLI, using three sizes of the Qwen3.5 model family. They compared it with two approaches that make a single revision per case, one of which can consult the web; both comparisons used the same feasibility checks.

items.content:
Training language models on sensitive data can expose personal or confidential information, while standard privacy-protecting training often performs poorly when only a few hundred private examples are available. The article addresses how to preserve a formal privacy guarantee without losing as much task performance in this small-data setting. It proposes PE-SGD, a method that uses synthetic examples to guide private model updates.

The article evaluates whether two changes can make private training more effective: adapting the synthetic examples as the model changes, rather than relying on a fixed set, and adding privacy noise at a more effective stage of the update. PE-SGD projects information from private-example gradients into a lower-dimensional space formed by synthetic-example gradients. It then evolves the synthetic set during training and adds noise to the final projection coefficients. The researchers tested the method on three language models and three text domains—biomedical abstracts, parliamentary speeches, and biology preprints—using as few as 400 private training examples. The main comparisons used a strict privacy setting, with a privacy budget of 1.

items.content:
Advertisement systems depend on accurate judgments about whether an ad answers a user’s query. Producing these labels by experts is costly and slow, while LLMs can miss the specialized context needed to judge relevance. The article addresses how to make automated labeling more accurate by giving language models better examples of previously labeled query–ad pairs.

The article introduces ICL-Bandit, a method that learns which examples to include in a language model’s prompt. It treats the choice of examples as a repeated selection problem: the system tests demonstrations, checks whether the model’s label matches a known expert label, and uses that feedback to improve future selections. The evaluation used 1.58 million expert-labeled examples as a demonstration pool, with separate, time-ordered training and test sets of about 10,000 and 2,000 pairs. The authors compared the method with common retrieval approaches and other learned methods, using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.

Experience and senior judgment should be consulted before critical enterprise decisions are made, not merely when those decisions encounter failure.

Independent decision-making carries independent accountability. Seeking senior expertise after the consequences emerge does not automatically transfer ownership of those decisions.

In high stakes AI deployments, prospective validation, risk assessment, stakeholder consultation, and clear decision ownership must precede implementation.

The lesson: Consult before you commit. Challenge assumptions. Own your decisions. Own their consequences.
